claims.text: Replacing explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics integration with a machine-learning interatomic potential combined with free-energy perturbation will substantially reduce computational cost.
The proposed method will retain sufficient fidelity to capture vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling.
A representative ab initio training set, particularly one emphasizing liquid configurations, can produce an adequate machine-learning potential for solid and liquid free-energy calculations.
Free-energy perturbation can compute the free energies of both solid and liquid states without full ab initio molecular-dynamics thermodynamic integration.
The method is applicable within approximately ±20% of the fusion temperature.
Elemental and binary validation can provide a basis for subsequent testing in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The machine-learning potential can efficiently represent the high-dimensional ab initio energy landscape.
The represented energy landscape will retain the physical interactions needed for vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions.
Accurate training on ab initio data will enable the machine-learning potential to simulate the relevant energy landscape with sufficient accuracy.
A post hoc free-energy perturbation correction will preserve the necessary thermodynamic information while avoiding costly explicit ab initio trajectories.
Free-energy differences and derived observables should agree with explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results to within approximately 5%.
The proposed approach should reduce computational cost and time by approximately one order of magnitude relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics.
The proposed approach should provide greater throughput than TOR-TILD.
The method is expected to work for elemental and binary systems having moderate vibrational and anharmonic effects near melting.
Extreme electron correlation may reduce the method's accuracy or applicability.
Complex high-entropy free-energy landscapes and electron–vibration couplings may limit potential transferability and accuracy in multicomponent systems.
